confidence_basis.high: Directly published curve from a peer-reviewed or agency source, with a substantial underlying sample in the region it is applied to.
confidence_basis.medium: Published curve, but the continental/regional average rests on few underlying functions, or the curve is applied outside the exact population it was fitted on.
confidence_basis.low: Published but thin: a generic global average of two or three regional curves, or a small-literature-base fragility. Treat as an order of magnitude, not a point estimate.
confidence_basis.note: Confidence describes how well-supported the curve is by its own source, not how well it fits any particular asset. Region and occupancy mismatch is a separate error, see gaps.

units.y: damage as a fraction of the relevant maximum damage value, 0-1
units.max_damage: Euro per m2 at 2010 price level; Infrastructure is Euro per m of road, Agriculture is Euro per m2 of agricultural land. null = not reported.

max_damage.source: Huizinga, De Moel & Szewczyk (2017), EUR 28552 EN / JRC105688, doi:10.2760/16510, Table 3-21 (per continent) and Table 3-22 (per country)
max_damage.units: EUR/m2, 2010 price level (see units.max_damage for exceptions)
max_damage.caveat: The JRC report flags several of these as implausibly high relative to peers and in need of further research (notably North American agriculture at 662 EUR/m2). Values are averages over few observations per country. Treat as indicative.

gaps.why: No credible public depth-equivalent damage function exists. physrisk-lib ships a single generic SPEI-12 stub (points_x [-3.5,-3.0,-2.5,-2.0], points_y [1.0,0.2,0.1,0.0]) which is a decreasing 4-point placeholder with no published calibration, not a vulnerability curve. Drought loss is mediated by water rights, storage and substitution, none of which a univariate hazard-to-damage curve captures.
gaps.what_would_close_it: Facility-level water-withdrawal and curtailment records joined to a basin water-stress index; or a published sector water-intensity elasticity.

gaps.why: No public wildfire vulnerability curve at asset-value-fraction resolution. physrisk-lib ships a single point (fire_probability 1.0 -> damage 0.7) with no source. Published wildfire fragility work is structure-specific (roof/vent/ember-defensible-space) and is not a function of a single hazard intensity variable, so it cannot be expressed in this schema honestly.
gaps.what_would_close_it: A burn-probability x structure-hardening matrix, e.g. from the USFS Wildfire Risk to Communities dataset plus NIST/IBHS ember-exposure testing.

gaps.why: physrisk-lib ships only two single-point stubs (days above 5 cm = 0.02 -> damage 0.001 generic, 0.3 for solar). A single point is not a curve and the underlying calibration is not published. Not included.
gaps.what_would_close_it: Insurer hail claims severity vs hailstone diameter, or IEC 61215 impact test data mapped to field diameters.

gaps.why: physrisk-lib ships a WBGT-days curve for ManufacturingAsset traceable to ILO (2019) 'Working on a warmer planet'. It is a real source, but its y-axis is productivity disruption, not damage to asset value, so it does not belong in a damage-fraction dataset. Excluded on units, not on credibility.
gaps.what_would_close_it: A separate disruption-curve dataset with its own units; the ILO curve can be lifted directly into it.

gaps.why: Hazus 6.1 huDamLossFun does provide a downtime function per building type, and physrisk exposes it, but its values reach 2.22 -- it is relative loss-of-use in days, not a 0-1 damage fraction. Excluded rather than rescaled into something it is not.
gaps.what_would_close_it: Include it in a downtime dataset with x_units days and no 0-1 bound.

gaps.exposure: Transport and Infrastructure outside Asia and South America
gaps.why: The JRC report found no usable damage functions for Transport in Africa, Oceania or North America, and none for Infrastructure outside Asia; it tells the user to fall back on the European curve or the generic global function. Those fallbacks are not separate empirical curves, so they are not emitted as distinct continental curves. Use jrc_flood_global_infrastructure or jrc_flood_global_agriculture, and note the substitution.
gaps.what_would_close_it: Continental road/rail damage surveys; none currently public at this resolution.

gaps.exposure: Commercial in Africa, Industrial in Oceania
gaps.why: The JRC report had no underlying damage functions for either and directs the reader to substitute the European curve. jrc_flood_africa_commercial and jrc_flood_oceania_industrial are therefore copies of the European curves, marked confidence 'low' with proxy_for = 'Europe'. They are present so the six-continent grid is complete, not because the data exists.
gaps.what_would_close_it: Loss data from African commercial and Oceanian industrial flood events.

gaps.why: The JRC and Hazus flood curves used here are freshwater/riverine. Salt water is more damaging to fabric and equipment, but no public curve quantifies the uplift globally. Applying the riverine curves to coastal flooding is a known under-estimate and is not corrected for here.
gaps.what_would_close_it: Hazus coastal V-zone functions with wave action, or post-event coastal loss data.

gaps.why: Every building-type wind curve here is Hazus, i.e. calibrated on US construction and US building codes. The Eberenz regional curves cover other regions but only at whole-asset generic resolution, not by building type. Do not read hazus_wind_* as valid for, say, Asian construction.
gaps.what_would_close_it: Regional wind vulnerability curves, e.g. GEM/GAR or national cyclone codes.
